public import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Prime Tuples Conjecture

*Reference:* [FLC07] Friedlander, J. B. and Luca, F. and Stoiciu, M., On the irrationality of a
divisor function series. Integers (2007).
-/

@[expose] public section

open Nat

namespace PrimeTuplesConjecture

/-- For any `k ≥ 2`, let `a₁,...,aₖ` and `b₁,...,bₖ` be integers with `aᵢ > 0`. Suppose that for
every prime `p` there exists an integer `n` such that `p ∤ ∏ i, (aᵢ n + bᵢ)`. Then there exist
infinitely many `n` such that `aᵢ n + bᵢ` is prime for all `i`. -/
@[category research open, AMS 11]
theorem prime_tuples_conjecture {k : ℕ} (hk : 2 ≤ k) (a : Fin k → ℕ+) (b : Fin k → ℕ)
    (hab : ∀ p, p.Prime → ∃ n, ¬ p ∣ ∏ i, (a i * n + b i)) :
    Set.Infinite {n | ∀ i : Fin k, (a i * n + b i).Prime} := by sorry

end PrimeTuplesConjecture

reformulations.difference: Conjecture 1 allows integer offsets bᵢ and integer witnesses in the local divisibility hypothesis, and concludes infinitude of positive integer solutions. Lean uses natural-number offsets and witnesses and permits n = 0 in the solution set.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: These universally quantified statements are equivalent. Given positive integer aᵢ and arbitrary integer bᵢ, choose c ≥ 0 so that Bᵢ = aᵢc + bᵢ ≥ 0 for every i. Substitution n = m + c preserves the integer local hypothesis. For each prime p, an integer witness can be reduced modulo p to a natural-number witness without changing divisibility of the product. Applying the Lean formulation to the Bᵢ gives infinitely many original solutions m + c; discarding m = 0 ensures positivity. Conversely, the source specializes to natural offsets, and its positive solutions are natural solutions. This full equivalence, including integer-valued aᵢ with explicit positivity hypotheses, was proved as PrimeTuplesReview.natForm_iff_sourceIntegerForm in /workspace/review/equivalence.lean, independently of the conjecture’s sorry proof.

sources_consulted: Friedlander, J. B., Luca, F., and Stoiciu, M., “On the Irrationality of a Divisor Function Series,” Integers 7 (2007), A31, especially Conjecture 1 on p. 3 and the discussion of Theorem 2: https://math.colgate.edu/~integers/h31/h31.pdf
